Thu 0230 Treasurer Costello at Economic Society, Melbourne
QUESTION OF THE WEEK - Following last week's benign

inflation report for the second quarter, which saw the policy sensitive annual underlying rate fall below the Reserve Bank's 2.0-3.0 percent target at 1.7 percent, economists were asked when would it get back to the danger level of 3.0 percent. The jury is still out as to whether Wednesday's 0.5 percentage point cut in official cash rates to 5.0 percent would be the last in the cycle, although last week's data showing a fall to 3.7 percent in the annual rate of wages growth does suggest that a low inflation environment is entrenched for now. And given economists' forecasts for future inflation growth it looks as if the RBA will have little to worry about over inflation pressures in the near future and policy could be on hold for some time once interest rates have bottomed. Forecasts were generally fairly evenly spread over 1999, although some estimates were looking towards the end of 1998 with the stimulus from the RBA's current easing bias beginning to impact on economic growth going into 1997 year-end
RETAIL SALES - Probably the most important release of the
week given the very erratic performance of sales in April and
May -- a 1.7 percent fall followed by a 2.9 percent rise.
The wide range of forecasts reflects this volatility as well
as uncertainty about the state of consumer demand in general.
Analysts noted vehicle sales were up strongly in the month -
registrations were at a record high - and consumer sentiment
looked to have improved following the May 23 interest rate cut.
Sales volumes in the quarter should be supported by the
very low level of the retail trade deflator, but not be enough
to see much a real rise on top of the hefty 2.2 percent gain
